source.title: Video Unlearning via Low-Rank Refusal Vector
source.authors: Simone Facchiano; Stefano Saravalle; Matteo Migliarini; Edoardo De Matteis; Alessio Sampieri; Andrea Pilzer; Emanuele Rodolà; Indro Spinelli; Luca Franco; Fabio Galasso

page_placements.theme: Safety and concept steering in video diffusion and physics models (analogues outside language models)

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the single-refusal-direction work and adapts difference-in-means vectors as a tool for targeted concept removal in video diffusion models. It reports how its own video-unlearning method performs, but does not test refusal behavior in safety-trained chat models.
record.gate_note: The paper derives unsafe-minus-safe activation vectors for video concepts, edits video-model weights, and reports unsafe-generation, quality, and semantic-alignment outcomes. These are results about concept suppression in video generation, not refusal or compliance behavior in chat models, so the rows are recorded under none. Some comparator and appendix results are omitted because they do not test the claim's chat-refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the difference-in-means 'refusal vector' idea (citing Arditi et al.) as a tool for concept erasure in text-to-video diffusion models (Open-Sora, ZeroScopeT2V). It reports only its own method's unsafe-generation rates, FVD, MM-Notox and FVMD. It measures no refusal or compliance behaviour in language or chat models and has no harmful-vs-harmless instruction direction. None of V1–V8 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that a training-free closed-form low-rank 'refusal vector' weight update reduces unsafe video generations (36.3% and 58.2% average reductions) while preserving video quality and prompt alignment. They make no claim about refusal mediation in language models.
record.recipe_differences: The method uses paired unsafe/safe activation differences and a projected direction, but applies contrastive low-rank refinement and a closed-form weight edit to selected video-diffusion layers rather than ablating or adding a residual-stream direction across every chat-model layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity to cPCA rank (best results at k = 100), suppression strength λ (larger values reduce unsafe content but very large values visibly corrupt video), and layer choice (layers 17–18 are described as most effective). Five prompt pairs are used; more than five reportedly gives no noticeable performance gain. Pair similarity and neutral-prompt resampling results are also reported as broadly stable.

fits_no_version.finding: In Open-Sora and ZeroScopeT2V, a closed-form low-rank weight edit built from five unsafe/safe prompt-pair difference vectors lowers GPT-4o-judged unsafe-generation rates. Open-Sora on T2VSafetyBench falls from 48.9% to 12.6% on average; ZeroScopeT2V on SafeSora falls from 68.1% to 9.9%. Average FVD is roughly unchanged, with some categories worse. The plain difference vector alone gives 44.7% to 18.0% (Pornography); cPCA refinement gives 13.4%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Difference-in-means concept vectors, folded into weights, can suppress unsafe visual concepts in text-to-video diffusion models with small quality cost.

record.problems: The reported safety evaluation uses GPT-4o automated judgments. No uncertainty estimates or statistical tests are stated for the reported tables. FVD, MM-Notox, and FVMD are proxies rather than broad tests of general capability; some category-level quality or alignment values worsen. Several appendix results use subsets, and the text does not state sample sizes for every table.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the NullSCE and SAFREE comparator entries in Tables 1–2, the cPCA-rank and λ figure-only sweeps, multi-vector combination results in Table 8, UCE adaptation results in Tables 9–10, α results in Table 11, and the adversarial-prompting result in Appendix H. These concern other methods, video concept-unlearning configurations, or video-generation attacks rather than the claimed chat-model refusal behavior; the paper's own method results most directly related to video unsafe-generation reduction and quality are retained above.

untested.parts: All of it. No refusal behaviour in LLMs; no harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction; no ablation of the direction or addition of it to induce refusal.
All of it. The weight edit erases visual concepts in video models; it does not remove refusal from released chat models.
All of it. Appendix H tests an adversarial attack against video concept erasure, not jailbreaks suppressing an LLM refusal direction.
All of it. The low-rank cPCA subspaces and multi-vector combinations concern video concept erasure, not the geometry of refusal.

record.verdict_notes: 'Refusal vector' here is borrowed terminology for a concept-erasure direction in diffusion models. The models do not refuse; they generate altered content. The reader's T4 / uses_without_test call and its none-linking of all rows are correct. The rows left out (comparators, multi-vector Table 8, UCE, α, adversarial) were properly declared and are not needed for the claim.

versions.untested_parts: Tests neither refusal nor harmful-request compliance in safety-trained chat models; does not ablate one residual-stream direction at every layer and position, add it to induce refusals, or evaluate general chat abilities.
Does not test an abliteration weight edit that removes refusals from released chat models.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed chat-model refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Its multi-vector concept-removal experiments concern video generation, not whether chat-model refusal is affine, conical, or carried by multiple directions.
Does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions in chat models.
Does not test transfer of the claimed chat refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Does not compare refusal training methods or stages in chat models.

unmatched_labels.reason: The systems are video diffusion models (Open-Sora, ZeroScopeT2V) and the behaviour is unsafe-content generation, not LLM refusal. No row bears on any version.

relation.reason: Cites Arditi et al. 2024 as motivation and borrows the mean-difference plus projection construction. Never tests whether a direction mediates refusal in an LLM.

tranche.reason: Adapts the Arditi et al. difference-in-means 'refusal vector' as a tool for concept erasure in text-to-video diffusion models. Reports only its own method's unsafe-generation rate, FVD, MM-Notox and FVMD. Measures no refusal or compliance in language models.

source_check.notes: The closest analogue to Arditi is Table 5 ('Refusal Only', plain mean-difference projection): Open-Sora Pornography 44.7% -> 18.0%, vs 13.4% with cPCA. It is still video diffusion, not LLM refusal. The Open-Sora checkpoint is implied to be the updated Open-Sora 2.0 (Xiangyu et al. 2025), with baselines recomputed. The layer description is inconsistent: section 5 says layers 17-18, but Appendix A says every double block (Open-Sora) and the up-blocks (ZeroScope). 'Censorship rate' means the % of unsafe videos (lower is better).

statements.correction: Table 1 averages: Open-Sora 48.9% -> Ours 12.6% on T2VSafetyBench. Table 2: ZeroScopeT2V 68.1% -> 9.9% on SafeSora. Judge: GPT-4o, binary per frame, aggregated per video. Refusal vector = mean of 5 unsafe/safe pair differences, refined by cPCA against about 1000 neutral prompts.
statements.problem: None. Minor omission: the cPCA step also uses about 1000 GPT-generated neutral prompts, besides the five pairs.
